newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FORECAST-NZ jobs data seen confirming slowdown.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-NZ jobs data seen confirming slowdown.

text.p: Employment data due on Tuesday should confirm cooling labour pressures, but financial markets may wait for wage statistics later in February before attempting to ease monetary conditions, economists said on Friday.
"The market is expecting the labour market to become a little bit softer, with employment slowing and unemployment rising," said Peter Scobie, economist at AMP.
"I think that's probably good news for the Reserve Bank and will leave it a little bit more comfortable about the way the economy is developing."
Economists expect the December quarter Household Labour Force Survey to reflect the slowdown in economic growth.

Twelve economists polled by Reuters on average expect seasonally-adjusted employment growth of 0.325 percent for the quarter. But surprisingly robust 0.8 percent growth in the September quarter, buoyed by a spike in part-time employment, prompted a wide range of forecasts, from zero to 0.6 percent.

"It's a bit of a mixed picture because full-time employment growth over both the June and September quarters was actually negative and all the growth is coming through the part-time side," said Hamish Macalister at WestpacTrust.
He said if part-time employment growth tailed off and full-time growth remained negative, the net effect could be a substantial overall decline.
David Plank at Bankers Trust said a low number for employment growth could initiate a market-led easing of conditions.

"If this number comes in around zero, I think the market will ease and that the Reserve Bank won't do anything about it," he said. But he was wary of the divergence between part and full-time employment statistics.
BNZ's Peter Jolly said the expectation was for another fall in full-time employment. But if part-time recorded another rise, the headline number could again surprise on the upside.
"At some point we might get a negative employment number -- most people have been forecasting that and we're continually getting beaten around the head by it," he said.

"The productivity numbers certainly suggest that there is some rationalisation in the labour market to occur, but it seems to be forever being delayed, and if it's consistent with recent history, it probably will be delayed again."

Robin Clements at SBC Warburg said that if employment growth failed to slow, the market could be left in something of a quandary: "Not only will you be squeezing productivity, but maybe ongoing employment growth is why consumer confidence held up," he said.
Most economists felt unemployment would continue to rise, with Ulf Schoefisch at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell predicting a rate of seven percent by the end of the year.

Most also agreed that the data were not in themselves likely to prompt an easing in conditions. "I think the market will probably sit and wait for the wages data just to get some confirmation that the pressures are abating," Scobie said.
The December Labour Cost Index is due on February 21, while the Quarterly Employment Survey comes out four days later.
